title: One grape, two names
subtitle: DNA and identity
objectives: Explain how Zinfandel and Primitivo were linked
Explain how its Croatian origin was found

steps.title: The DNA story
steps.body: For years, Zinfandel was thought to be an American grape. In the 1970s, a professor noticed Primitivo in Puglia looked similar; in 1994, DNA showed they were identical. Dr Carole Meredith of UC Davis then searched Croatia; in 2001 she confirmed Crljenak Kaštelanski as the same grape, and later found an older name, Tribidrag, recorded in the 15th century.

steps.title: Labelling
steps.body: Since the EU and the US recognised them as the same, Italian producers can label Primitivo as Zinfandel when exporting to the US, and US producers can call theirs Primitivo. Still, the two are made in different styles: Puglian Primitivo tends to be softer and more rustic; Californian Zinfandel bolder and fruitier.

steps.explanation: Dr Carole Meredith of UC Davis led the DNA research in Croatia.

steps.title: Tribidrag
steps.body: Tribidrag was mentioned in Croatian documents from the 1400s. Phylloxera and neglect almost wiped it out there. Since the DNA discovery, Croatian producers have replanted it on the Dalmatian coast. It's a reminder that wine grapes travel and change names along the way.

steps.prompt: Zinfandel was originally an American grape.
steps.explanation: Not true. DNA shows it came from Croatia, where it was known as Tribidrag.

steps.title: What you learned
points: DNA showed Zinfandel and Primitivo are identical in 1994
Its Croatian origin, Tribidrag, was confirmed in 2001
Labelling rules allow both names, though styles differ
